topics.name: Fractions
topics.summary: Parts of a whole: naming, comparing and adding fractions.

objectives.text: Name the numerator and denominator of a fraction.
Compare two fractions with the same denominator.

keyTerms.definition: A number describing part of a whole that has been cut into equal parts.
The top number: how many parts you have.
The bottom number: how many equal parts the whole was cut into.
Pieces of exactly the same size. Without this, a fraction has no meaning.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
A fraction is not one number — it is two numbers doing two different jobs.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

• name the numerator and the denominator, and say what each one tells you
• work out what fraction of a whole is left over
• compare two fractions that have the same denominator, and explain why

sections.heading: The two numbers
sections.body:
A fraction has a top number and a bottom number. The bottom number — the denominator — tells you how many equal parts the whole has been cut into. The top number — the numerator — tells you how many of those parts you have.

The word EQUAL is doing a lot of work here. If a loaf is cut into 8 pieces of different sizes, taking 3 of them is not 3/8 of the loaf. A fraction only means something when the parts are the same size.

One way to hold the two words apart: the Denominator is Down, and it tells you how many pieces the whole was Divided into.
sections.example:
If a loaf is cut into 8 equal slices and you take 3, you have 3/8 of the loaf. The 8 is the denominator, the 3 is the numerator.

The rest of the loaf is the other 5 slices, which is 5/8. Notice that 3/8 and 5/8 together make 8/8 — one whole loaf.

sections.heading: Comparing fractions
sections.body:
When two fractions have the same denominator, the pieces are the same size, so the one with the bigger numerator is bigger. 5/8 is greater than 3/8 because five equal pieces beat three of the same size.

This only works when the denominators match. Comparing 3/8 with 1/2 by looking at the top numbers would tell you 3/8 is bigger, and that is wrong: 1/2 is 4/8.

So before you compare, check the bottoms. Same denominator — compare the tops. Different denominators — you cannot compare them directly yet.
sections.example:
Which is bigger, 7/10 or 4/10?

Both wholes were cut into 10 equal parts, so every piece is the same size. Seven pieces is more than four.

    7/10 > 4/10

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body:
A cassava is cut into 12 equal pieces. Musu takes 5 pieces and Sia takes 4.

(a) What fraction does each girl have?

    The whole was cut into 12 equal parts, so 12 is the denominator for both.
    Musu: 5 pieces → 5/12
    Sia:  4 pieces → 4/12

(b) Who has more?

    The denominators are the same, so the pieces are the same size.
    Compare the numerators: 5 > 4.
    Musu has more.

(c) What fraction is left?

    Taken altogether: 5 + 4 = 9 pieces.
    Left: 12 − 9 = 3 pieces → 3/12

(d) Check.

    5/12 + 4/12 + 3/12 = 12/12, which is the whole cassava. ✓

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.body:
**Reading the fraction upside down.** In 3/8 you have 3 pieces out of 8, not 8 pieces out of 3. Denominator is Down.

**Forgetting that the parts must be equal.** Three of eight uneven pieces is not 3/8.

**Comparing tops when the bottoms differ.** 3/8 looks bigger than 1/2 if you only read the numerators, but 1/2 is the same as 4/8, so 1/2 wins.

**Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction.** More pieces means SMALLER pieces. 1/12 is less than 1/4.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. In the fraction 5/9, name the numerator and the denominator.

2. A pizza is cut into 6 equal slices and you eat 2. What fraction did you eat? What fraction is left?

3. Which is bigger, 4/7 or 6/7? Say why.

4. Can you tell straight away which is bigger, 2/3 or 2/5? What is different about this question?

5. A rope is cut into 10 equal pieces. Three are used. Write the fraction used and the fraction left, and check they add to 10/10.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• The denominator (bottom) says how many equal parts the whole was cut into.
• The numerator (top) says how many of those parts you have.
• The parts must be EQUAL or the fraction means nothing.
• With the same denominator, the bigger numerator is the bigger fraction.
• With different denominators, you cannot compare the tops directly.

questions.question: In the fraction 3/8, which number is the denominator?
questions.explanation: The denominator is the bottom number. It tells you how many equal parts the whole was cut into - here, 8.

questions.question: Which fraction is larger: 5/8 or 3/8?
questions.explanation: The denominators match, so the pieces are the same size. Five pieces is more than three, so 5/8 is larger.

questions.question: A loaf is cut into 8 equal slices. You take 3. What fraction of the loaf is left?
questions.explanation: Eight slices in total, three taken, so five remain. That is 5/8 of the loaf.
